title: Routing policy dependency and consistency retrospective
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures notes and decisions from the 2025-11-07 architecture retrospective focused on routing policy dependencies and consistency guarantees across runtime components. The goal was to reconcile prior RFC assumptions with observed operational issues during the October incident and to propose concrete rollout and mitigation steps for the next sprint.

Attendees:
- Nina Morales (owner, notes)
- Ethan Liu
- Priya Kothari
- Samir Rao
- Jasper Nguyen
- Olivia Park
- On-call SRE: Mei Zhang (joined for incident context)

Agenda:
1) Quick incident recap and where routing policy surfaced as a contributing factor
2) Surface implicit coupling between policy evaluation and KV cache/batching
3) Evaluate alternatives for consistency and latency trade-offs
4) Decide on versioning/rollout approach and canary criteria
5) Assign actions and timeline

Incident recap (summary):
- During an October regional disruption, the routing service returned a stale policy for ~12 minutes in eu-west and caused a spike in cold KV cache misses because session affinity shifted unexpectedly.
- The cascade: policy server mesh reconfiguration -> short window where older policy could be served -> sticky affinity flip -> model variant mismatch -> KV cache miss -> CPU/latency spike on hosts that had to refill caches.
- Root cause: policy publishing and cache invalidation paths were not strongly ordered; there were race windows where nodes accepted new connections but continued using prior policy semantics.

Problems identified (high level):
- Implicit coupling: routing policy evaluation is tightly coupled to (a) session affinity decisions, (b) KV cache shard placement, and (c) upstream batching heuristics. Changes in policy semantics can change the sharding affinity and invalidate warm state.
- Lack of transactional publication: no single atomic publish that ensures all components transition together.
- Rollout blind spots: canarying on a single metric (error-rate) missed gradual increases in cache-miss tail latency.

Design constraints and goals:
- Maintain existing per-session sticky affinity semantics for conversational workloads to maximize KV cache hits and minimize token-cost churn.
- Keep 99th-percentile tail latency impact within existing SLO budget (target: <5% deviation during rollout).
- Ensure ability to rapidly rollback and forward-fix without producing inconsistent policy application across a customer session.
- Minimal client-side changes; prefer server-side backward-compatible transitions.

Alternatives discussed:
A) Strongly ordered publish with two-phase commit across policy + cache controllers
- Pros: deterministic transition; nodes either see old or new policy and corresponding cache invalidation state.
- Cons: operationally heavy; requires leader coordination and slows publish latency; failure modes where commit stalls could prevent rollouts.

B) Versioned policy with session-binding token (preferred v1)
- Idea: publish new policy as version vN. Clients/routers bind ongoing sessions to the policy version they observed at session creation. New sessions can opt into vN once canary pass is green. Cache keys include policy-version so warm state is isolated.
- Pros: isolates cache traffic across versions, avoids mid-session flips, easy rollback by shifting new session routing back to vN-1.
- Cons: increased cache duplication during rollouts (temporary memory and miss penalty), requires cache key convention change and small instrumentation changes for visibility.

C) Lazy migration with affinity drift guard
- Idea: allow policy evaluation changes but gate affinity flips by threshold (only flip if session is idle or after explicit checkpoint).
- Pros: less cache duplication, lower publish complexity.
- Cons: more complicated heuristics, can lead to long-lived mismatches if sessions remain active for long periods.

D) Publish-with-compatibility-layer
- Idea: policy layer exposes compatibility flags and the serving runtime supports legacy and new semantics concurrently. Requires runtime branching.
- Pros: zero-downtime transition is possible.
- Cons: increased complexity in runtime, more code paths to maintain and test.

Decision (consensus):
- Adopt alternative B as the primary approach for the next iteration: versioned policy + session-binding token + cache-key namespacing. Label this release "Routing Policy Versioning v1". Rationale: provides deterministic per-session behavior, simplifies rollback, and limits blast radius even if it temporarily increases cache size during rollout. It aligns with the platform philosophy of predictable, observable transitions.

Detailed design notes for v1:
- Policy publish flow:
  1) Policy authored and validated in control plane -> assigned incremented semantic version (e.g., policy:42).
  2) Policy artifact stored in policy-store with version metadata and SHA.
  3) Publish command triggers config plane to mark version as "canary" for a subset of routing tiers.
  4) Routers include observed-policy-version in session-creation response and embed policy-version in session token (signed).
- Runtime changes:
  - Accept session tokens that contain policy-version; if absent, default to current stable version.
  - Cache key format: <policy-version>::<model-range>::<session-id-prefix>::<prompt-prefix-hash>
  - When a router receives a request with an older policy-version, it routes the request to model variant and KV shard consistent with that version.
- Observability and instrumentation:
  - Emit metrics: policy.version.binding_count, cache.misses.by_policy_version, route.mismatch_count
  - Tracing: add policy.version tag to request traces and sampled KV refill traces.
- Canary strategy and SLOs:
  - Canary group = 1% of sessions by user-segmentation, across 3 regions (us-east1, eu-west, ap-south).
  - Canary pass criteria: no more than 2% increase in cache.miss-rate, <3% increase in 99p latency, zero increase in model-mismatch errors for 30m continuous window.
  - If criteria fail, automatic rollback to previous stable version for new sessions; ongoing sessions remain bound to whichever version they have.
- Rollback semantics:
  - Rolling back will stop marking new sessions for vN and mark vN-1 as current. No forced rebinding for active sessions; we rely on session lifetime to drain. For urgent fixes we will provide a migration tool to explicitly reassign sessions when safe.

Open questions and risks:
- Cost of cache duplication at high QPS customers vs SLO benefit. Need a cost model per customer class.
- Edge cases where sessions are short-lived but high throughput — duplication may be less of an issue, but transitional pressure on cache refill path could still cause CPU spikes.
- Do we need a soft-eviction policy for old-version caches to limit memory pressure? Operate as LRU with version-aware aging.
- Can third-party integrations (e.g., private deployments with restricted publish cadence) interoperate with versioned policies? Need compatibility modes for private deployment control planes.

Action items (owners and ETA):
1) Prototype cache key namespacing and session-token binding in kanary sandbox. Owner: Priya Kothari. ETA: 2025-11-21.
2) Implement metric set and tracing tags for policy.version. Owner: Jasper Nguyen. ETA: 2025-11-14.
3) Build canary orchestration script that marks policy versions canary/active and evaluates pass criteria. Owner: Ethan Liu. ETA: 2025-11-28.
4) Run cost modeling exercise for cache duplication scenarios (by customer tier). Owner: Samir Rao + Finance consult. ETA: 2025-11-18.
5) Draft runbook additions for rollback and migration tool usage. Owner: Olivia Park. ETA: 2025-11-17.
6) Update RFC-2025-routing-policy with chosen design and compatibility notes for private deployments. Owner: Nina Morales. ETA: 2025-11-12.

Follow-ups planned:
- Weekly check-in for the next 3 weeks to review prototype metrics and canary readiness (invite list = eng-serving-runtime, eng-observability, SRE).
- Schedule a dry-run internal canary with non-critical customer traffic before any public rollout.

Appendix: quick notes on alternatives we discarded after discussion:
- Two-phase commit across policy + cache controllers (A) rejected due to operational fragility and longer publish times. Keep as a tech debt item to re-evaluate if we need stronger atomicity guarantees in future.
- Lazy migration with affinity drift guard (C) considered but delayed; may be useful as v2 if duplication costs become prohibitive.
- Compatibility layer (D) flagged as complex and deprioritized; still useful pattern for private/on-prem where we cannot quickly change runtime.

Meeting artifacts and refs:
- RFC-2025-routing-policy (linked above)
- Incident postmortem Oct-23-2025 (confluence://postmortem-2025-10-routing)
- GH-PR-3945 (routing policy versioning prototype)

Notes to reviewers: please comment inline on the canary thresholds (especially 99p latency delta) and on the proposed cache key format. If you foresee major pushback from platform teams about token size or trace overhead, flag early — we want to iterate now rather than late in implementation.

End of notes.
